title: Sound only
objective: Hear and produce the sounds English doesn't have. No grammar this week — it has the highest long-term leverage of the four months.
tasks: Record a 2-minute voice memo about yourself in whatever French you have (Gate 1 compares against it)
Book ONE 30-min italki community-tutor session as an assessment (Tue or Wed)
Install Anki + the 5000-word deck: Canadian audio variant, never hide the article field

steps.title: Why sound comes first
steps.body:
You **cannot recognise in speech what you have never correctly produced**. If you read French with English phonics, your listening score gets capped by pronunciation, not vocabulary.
So this week: sound only. It will feel like it isn't language learning. It is the week with the most leverage.

steps.q: Your reading is ahead of your speaking. What does that most likely cap first?
steps.explain: The ear can only match sounds it has stored correctly. That's why weeks 1–2 are phonetics — compressing them is the one economy that would cost you the exam.

steps.title: The vowel English doesn't have: u
steps.body:
Say "ee". Keep your tongue exactly there. Now round your lips as if for "oo". That's French **u**.
**ou** is the English "oo".
Click each: [[tu]] / [[tout]] · [[rue]] / [[roue]] · [[vu]] / [[vous]] · [[dessus]] / [[dessous]] · [[pu]] / [[pou]]

steps.prompt: In your own words: how do you physically make the French **u**? (One or two sentences.)
steps.model: Tongue forward and high as for "ee", lips tightly rounded as for "oo" — never a glide.

steps.title: No diphthongs
steps.body:
*The* anglophone error, and almost nobody is told. English vowels glide — "no" is really *now-oo*. French vowels are **pure, short, and stop**.
[[beau]] is one sound, held briefly. Same for [[mot]], [[nez]], [[café]].
Fixing this alone makes you markedly more comprehensible.

steps.title: é versus è
steps.body:
**é** is closed and tight (smile a little): [[été]].
**è / ê / ai** is open (jaw drops): [[est]], [[fête]], [[lait]].
Pairs: [[les]] / [[lait]] · [[ses]] / [[sait]] · [[été]] / [[était]]

steps.q: An English speaker says **beau** like "bow-oo". What's wrong?
options: The vowel glides into a second sound
steps.explain: French vowels don't glide. One pure sound, then stop.

steps.title: The three nasal vowels
steps.body:
Air through the nose, **no n or m sound at the end**.
[[banc]] / [[bon]] / [[bain]]
[[vent]] / [[vont]] / [[vingt]]
[[lent]] / [[long]] / [[lin]]
**Produce three, not four.** Most modern speakers merge *un* into *in* — recognise it, never worry about it.

steps.title: The R
steps.body:
Uvular — back of the throat, nothing to do with the tongue tip. Think of a light gargle.
Easiest **after a consonant**: [[trois]] · [[très]] · [[grand]] · [[France]]
Then **between vowels**: [[Paris]] · [[merci]]
Word-initial last: [[rouge]] · [[rien]]
Don't chase it. It arrives over two to three weeks.

steps.title: Silent endings
steps.body:
Final consonants are usually silent: [[petit]] · [[grand]] · [[vous]].
The killer: **-ent on a 3rd-person plural verb is silent**. [[ils parlent]] sounds exactly like [[il parle]].

steps.q: How do **il parle** and **ils parlent** differ when spoken?
options: You hear the s in ils
steps.explain: Identical (unless a vowel follows *ils* and triggers liaison: *ils‿aiment*). You'll rely on context in the listening paper.

steps.title: Shadowing — done properly
steps.body:
Most people do this wrong and get nothing from it.
1. Take a 30-second clip you **already understand** (Coffee Break French S1).
2. Play it again and speak **simultaneously** — chase the audio, don't repeat after it.
3. Record yourself. 4. Play both back. **The gap you hear is the lesson.**
15 minutes a day, all four months.

steps.title: Shadow the minimal pairs
steps.task: Click ▶ Model, then read the whole line aloud with it. Record once. Play yours back straight after the model.
steps.prompt: tu / tout · rue / roue · vu / vous · banc / bon / bain · vent / vont / vingt · trois · très · Paris · merci · rouge
steps.say: tu, tout. rue, roue. vu, vous. banc, bon, bain. vent, vont, vingt. trois, très, Paris, merci, rouge.

steps.title: Week-1 baseline (do it once)
steps.task: Two minutes, talking about yourself in whatever French you have. It will be bad — that's the point. **Save the recording.** Gate 1 asks for clear movement against it.
steps.prompt: Qui êtes-vous ? Où habitez-vous ? Quel est votre travail ?

steps.title: Your tutor assessment (book it now)
steps.body:
Not a lesson. Say explicitly:
*"I want an assessment, not teaching. Read a short text with me, correct every sound, and tell me which three sounds to work on."*
Write those three sounds down. Book it **Tuesday or Wednesday** — never on post-call Monday.

points: No diphthongs: one pure vowel, then stop
Three nasals to produce: an/en · on · in
R from the back of the throat, easiest after a consonant

items.q: Which audio variant should you pick in the Anki deck?
items.explain: TCF Canada audio is Canadian-facing. Free now, expensive to retrofit in January.

items.q: How should you learn the noun *chose*?
items.explain: Every noun with its article, from day one. Retrofitting gender onto 4,000 nouns is the most expensive avoidable mistake.
